question: Can pretrained code LLMs be adapted to make high-level, correctness-preserving performance improvements to C++ programs, measured reproducibly?
hypothesis: Data-driven adaptation using human performance-improving edits (retrieval prompting, finetuning, performance conditioning, self-play data) lets LLMs optimize code beyond what plain prompting or compilers achieve.
contributions: A dataset of more than 77K C++ program pairs (PIE) with execution times from the gem5 simulator
An evaluation of prompting and fine-tuning approaches for program optimization
Three adaptation strategies: retrieval-based prompting, performance-conditioning, self-play

method.summary: PIE pairs slow and fast accepted CodeNet C++ submissions by the same programmer (>10% faster), re-timed in gem5 (Skylake). Prompting (instruction, 2-shot, CoT, retrieval K shots) and fine-tuning (full, HQ subset, performance-conditioned, synthetic self-play) are compared on 978 held-out pairs using %Opt, Speedup and %Correct with Best@k sampling.

datasets.name: PIE train
datasets.source: CodeNet (Puri et al., 2021) accepted C++ submissions; extra tests from AlphaCode
datasets.preprocessing: pairs (y_i,y_j) within one user's accepted trajectory with relative time improvement >10%; timings relabelled in gem5; median 82.5 tests/problem

datasets.name: PIE test
datasets.preprocessing: median 104 tests/problem; fastest human submission time recorded per problem

datasets.name: PIE HQ subset
datasets.preprocessing: highest-speedup examples, max 4 pairs per problem, average 2.77 pairs/problem

datasets.name: Synthetic self-play
datasets.size: 1,485 optimized synthetic pairs (3,314 unique programs before filtering)
datasets.source: GPT-3.5 generated programs optimized by GPT-3.5 fine-tuned on PIE
datasets.preprocessing: keep pairs at least 5x faster, at most 3 semantic duplicates; 6,553 of 10,000 attempts not in PIE; HQ+self-play GPT-3.5 set is 5,570 pairs (footnote 4)

other.use: prompted and fine-tuned via OpenAI API

training.objective: supervised fine-tuning slow→fast; performance-conditioned variant prepends a 1-10 score tag to the fast program
training.epochs: 1 epoch for full-data and perf-cond; HQ until convergence
training.hardware: 8x 48GB GPUs (NVIDIA RTX A6000 / L40), HuggingFace Transformers with FSDP
training.compute: HQ under 12 hours with 8 GPUs; full and perf-cond 24 to 36 hours

other.scope: CodeLlama 7B and 13B only; GPT-3.5 fine-tuned through OpenAI API with no hyperparameters stated
other.perf_tags: top 10% of solutions per task are 10/10, next 10% 9/10, etc; inference uses 10/10
other.synthetic_gen: GPT-3.5 temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9, n=5 per prompt; 6 configs swept; 1.4M binary input pairs executed on 24-core Intel 13900k, 64GB RAM, under 72 hours

inference.decoding: sampling; Best@k = fastest of k samples that passes all tests
inference.samples: k=1 and k=8 (up to 40 for the fastest-possible-speedup comparison); no seeds or repeated runs stated
inference.prompting: instruction-only; 2-shot fixed random pairs; CoT with 2-shot; dynamic retrieval K in {1,2,4} (K=4 preferred)
inference.retrieval: CodeBertScore embeddings + FAISS nearest K programs from train, formatted slow→fast

metrics.name: %Opt
metrics.definition: fraction of 978 test programs that are correct and at least 10% faster

metrics.name: Speedup
metrics.definition: old time / new time averaged over all test examples; incorrect or slower outputs count as 1.0

eval.protocol: gem5 full-system simulator, Verbatim Intel Skylake config, GCC 9.3.0 C++17 -O3, two-minute timeout; deterministic so no repeated timing; no significance tests stated

prompts.text:
Given the program below, improve its performance:
### Program:
{src_code}
### Optimized Version:

slow1 →fast1 || slow2 →fast2 || slow3 →fast3 || ... || slowN →fastN
### Program:
{src_code}
### Optimized Version:

### slower program:
{src_code}
Give a potential strategy improving the program:
LLM reasoning: ...
### optimized version of the same code with the strategy mentioned above:

Below is a program. Optimize the program and provide a more efficient version.
### Program:
{src_code}
### Optimized Version:

This is a slow program we want to optimize to score 10/10.
### Program:
{src_code}
### Optimized Version:

evidence.quote: we used a batch size of 32 and a learning rate of 1e−5 for all of the experiments
BEST@k to denote this strategy with k samples and a temperature of 0.7

results.claim: Best model (GPT-3.5 fine-tuned on HQ + self-play data) reaches mean speedup 6.86x at Best@8, above the average human 3.66x.
results.setup: PIE test set, 978 pairs from 41 problems, gem5 Skylake, Best@8, temperature 0.7, speedup floored at 1.0 for incorrect/slower outputs
results.quote: a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 augmented with synthetic data via self-play achieves an average speedup of 6.86×

results.claim: Same model optimizes 87.63% of the test set by at least 10%.
results.setup: GPT-3.5 HQ + Self-Play, Best@8, PIE test
results.quote: optimizes 87.63% of the test set by at least 10%

results.claim: Fine-tuned CodeLlama 13B with performance-conditioned generation reaches 5.65x at Best@8.
results.setup: Full PIE train set (77,967 pairs), 1 epoch, Best@8
results.table: Table 4, row All w/Perf-Cond CODELLAMA 13B, column Best@8 Speedup

results.claim: Best retrieval-prompted model is GPT-4 with K=4 at 3.93x, 76.07% opt, Best@8.
results.setup: Prompting only, CodeBertScore + FAISS retrieval of K=4 pairs from train
results.table: Table 3, row Dynamic Retrieval K=4 GPT-4, column Best@8 Speedup

results.claim: Best prompting baseline (CoT) tops out at 1.60x average speedup over 8 samples versus 3.66x human reference.
results.quote: our strongest baseline COT only warrants a 1.60× average speedup over 8 submissions vs. the 3.66× human reference

results.claim: Model's fastest generations set a new upper limit of 9.64x versus 9.56x for the fastest human submissions.
results.setup: Test set, 39,129 model generations vs 118,841 accepted human CodeNet solutions; model sampled up to 40 samples
results.quote: the best human speedup achieved was 9.56×, while our model achieved a slightly higher speedup of 9.64×

results.setup: 500 identical slow/fast pairs benchmarked with hyperfine; true ratio 1
results.quote: observed a mean speedup of 1.12×, with a standard deviation of 0.36

results.quote: a speedup of 2.44× is reported, despite the programs and environments being identical

results.table: Table 2, row Instruction-Only GPT-3.5 vs Few-Shot GPT-3.5, column Best@8 Speedup

results.claim: Manual analysis of 120 edits: algorithmic changes 34.15%, I/O 26.02%, data structures 21.14%, misc 18.70%; 10 of 120 speedups came from shrinking array constants (spurious).
results.setup: 120 random pairs from GPT-3.5 HQ + self-play outputs, manual
results.quote: Algorithmic changes (complex modifications, such as changing recursive methods to dynamic programming, and unexpected ones, such as omitting Binary Indexed Trees for simpler constructs) are most common, comprising ~34.15% of changes

results.claim: Error analysis: 27.59% of failed outputs compiled but got 95-100% of test cases wrong; 12.51% failed to compile.
results.table: Table 5, row Compiled, but got [95-100%] of test cases wrong

limits: C++ competitive-programming programs only; test set is 41 problems.
Correctness is only 'passes the available tests'; 10 of 120 inspected speedups came from shrinking array constants, so tests may not cover all cases.
Two-minute gem5 timeout may add slight variability; altering it could change results.
GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 fine-tuning limited by cost and availability; GPT-4 not fine-tuned; CodeLlama 34B not fine-tuned.
Single run per configuration, no seeds or confidence intervals stated.
